channel.title: Audio Overviews
channel.description: Two-host audio overviews written by Claude and voiced by Gemini, made for personal listening.
channel.itunes:author: AI generated

item.title: Post-training: how a text predictor becomes a model you can use
item.description: The three kinds of lessons that turn a pretrained language model into an assistant: worked examples (SFT), comparisons (DPO) and practice with an answer key (reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards). Plus what reinforcement learning really changes, reward hacking, on-policy distillation, and new 2026 research.

item.title: The Emperor's New Mind: can a machine see what's true?
item.description: A deep dive into Roger Penrose's 1989 book: his Gödel argument that understanding isn't computation, the objections to it, his bet on gravity and quantum collapse, and what the evidence says now. Made with AI: script by Claude, voices by Gemini.

item.title: How NitroGen turns static into a button press
item.description: Why a game-playing model starts every decision from random noise: flow matching, the velocity field, and what each denoising step computes, read from the NitroGen source code. Script by Claude, voices by Gemini.

item.title: If pixels are too noisy to predict, why does diffusion work?
item.description: JEPA says don't predict pixels; diffusion models do it all day. Why both are right: 'noisy' means uncertain, and language models, diffusion and JEPA each escape the blur differently (list, sample, delete). Plus latent diffusion, REPA and pixel-space diffusion.

item.title: The world model was fine, the planner was lost: 600 experiments on a JEPA world model
item.description: A deep dive into a 600-experiment study of the LeWM JEPA world model on Push-T: why perfect physics didn't help, why planning breaks past about 25 steps, and four training-free fixes (subgoals, a memory graph, symmetry, and ignoring the pusher). Based on public summaries of the write-up and the LeWM paper.

item.title: The experts that aren't: what mixture-of-experts models really learn
item.description: MoE experts are not doctors in a hospital. A first-principles look at what routers and experts actually specialize in, from Mixtral's routing analysis to this year's interpretability work, and where the evidence is still contested.

item.title: The avalanche that hit math, and why AI research is next
item.description: Two hosts walk through an essay arguing that AI research is about to be automated, the way math problems suddenly fell to AI, and why that could mean superintelligence by 2030.

item.title: Robot by postcard: how a harness took Qwen from 2 to 31
item.description: A deep dive into uni-robot-agent, an open harness that lets a general AI model steer a robot through tool calls. Why the same open model went from 1.90 to 31.39 on RoboDojo, what the comparison with GPT-6 Astra really shows, and where the caveats are.

item.title: Expert weights as a compass: the P²-MOPD distillation paper
item.description: How learnable mixing coefficients on frozen expert task vectors make multi-teacher on-policy distillation faster and far more balanced, plus where the evidence is thin.

item.title: e-means: k-means in a tenth of the epochs
item.description: A deep dive into Meta FAIR's e-means paper: how mini-batch updates with exponential moving averages match 25 epochs of Lloyd's k-means in about two, what the evidence shows, and where the caveats are.

item.title: Training without backprop: from 1.76 hours to 1.6 seconds
item.description: How the Noise speedrun made forward-only training of a small GPT about 4,000 times faster in ten days, from random activation nudges to Hadamard probes and identity-path credit, and what it does and doesn't say about scaling.

item.title: Homeopathic learning: when clean data makes the poison stronger
item.description: A November 2026 paper (Clarke, Dubiński, Chua, Schrodi, Evans, Cloud) finds that poisoned fine-tuning data which does almost nothing alone can create a hidden backdoor once clean, contrasting data is mixed in. Covers the German-numbers, reward-hacking, bird-name and MNIST experiments, the blame-assignment explanation, and the limits.

item.title: How LLMs watch video: beyond sampling frames
item.description: Why the default is one frame per second, and the ideas that go beyond frame sampling: tokens that span time, pruning what did not move, reading the video codec, timestamps, audio, streaming and agentic viewing.

item.title: What attention actually computes
item.description: How a transformer works out what the word 'it' refers to: queries, keys and values, the dot product, and why attention is a soft search that can be trained.
